comments.body:
Under `dynamic=True`, two equal sizes are unified to one symbol, so an arg-reduction index can contain a power (`ks1**2 * x0 + x1`). Sympy is allowed to write that. The CPU C++ backend then drops it into the kernel with Python `str()`:

- `reduction_combine`: `f"{reduction_type}_combine(..., {index})"`
- vectorized path: `arg_extra = f", {self._adjust_argreduce_index(index)}"`

`str(expr)` uses `**`, which is not C++ (MSVC `C2100`, GCC unary `*`). The reduction itself is fine — the kernel never builds. Triton uses a different printer, so CUDA is unaffected. Static shapes, `amin`/`amax` (no index), and distinct inner sizes never produce that power, which is why the failure looks shape-depend

title: [inductor] `binary_cross_entropy` with a weight of another dtype and `huber_loss` with mixed low-precision inputs return float32 under Inductor; eager and aot_eager return the input dtype
Backward of `F.pdist` on an input with zero rows crashes the process (SIGSEGV on Linux, integer division by zero on Windows), no Python exception

prs.title: [pdist] Fix process crash in pdist backward for zero-row inputs
prs.author: SepehrRezaee

comments.body:
Root cause
- Forward of pdist on (0, d) is handled: Distance.cpp fills an empty result.
- Backward is not. apply_backward_pdist is documented as assuming a nonempty self.
- run_backward_parallel_pdist uses GRAIN_SIZE / (8 * n * n). For n == 0 that is integer division by zero (Windows STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO / Linux SIGSEGV). No Python exception.

Approach
- In apply_backward_pdist (or _pdist_backward), if self.size(0) == 0, leave the zero-filled result and return. Do not enter parallel_for.
- Do not change the nonempty path.

Tests
- n=0, d>0: backward returns zeros, process stays alive.
- n=1 and n=2 still match current behavior.
- Run the n=0 case in a subprocess so a crash is a test

comments.body:
Root-caused this to the Welford lowering path in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`, and the scope table in the report falls out of the path selection logic exactly.

Why only the scalar full reduction is affected: `use_two_step_variance()` returns False exactly when the output is a scalar (`sympy_product(ranges) == 1` early-returns False), so `var_mean` on a `(0,)` input goes through `var_mean_welford_()`, while reducing an empty dim on a `(0, 3)` input takes the two-step `var_mean_sum_()` path.

In `var_mean_welford_()` the mean output is the raw Welford accumulator from `ir.WelfordReduction.create()`. On an empty reduction the accumulator never leaves its identity state (mean=0, m2=0, count=0)

comments.body:
I looked into this.

For `x @ w`, AOT saves `permute(x)` for backward, not `x` itself. Eager `aten.permute` is a real view, so it shares `x`’s `version_counter_`. `x.add_(1)` between forward and backward bumps that counter and autograd raises, which is the point of the check.

title: [inductor] Floating-point floor division is off by one: `torch.compile` makes `1.0 // 0.1` return `10.0` (eager and Python: `9.0`)

comments.body:
I’d like to take this.

Floor division is not `floor` of a rounded quotient. `0.1` is stored slightly above 1/10, so the exact `1.0 / 0.1` is just below 10. IEEE `div_rn` rounds that to `10.0`, and `floor(10.0)` is 10. Python and eager both return 9, because they use remainder: `mod = fmod(a, b)`, then `floor((a - mod) / b)`, which cannot overshoot the integer.

`_floor_div_floating` in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` does `floor(ops.div_rn(a, b))`. That is why inductor is off by one on every quotient that sits just below an integer but rounds up (`0.5 // 0.1`, `6.0 // 0.2` as well). `aot_eager` matches eager, so this is the inductor lowering, not Dynamo.

comments.body:
Opened #40842 with a fix and a regression test.

The loop now runs on unsigned magnitudes (your first suggestion) and converts back on exit; the conversion wraps `gcd(INT_MIN, 0)` to `INT_MIN`, matching NumPy. Verified against NumPy over every ordered pair from `{min, min+1, -6, -1, 0, 1, 2, 6, 12, 18, 128, max-1, max}` for int8/16/32/64 and uint8/16/32/64, eager and jit, with x64 on — no mismatches.

Thanks for the report! Just a note that the `gcd` issue was recently fixed in NumPy as well: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/31379, so I suspect JAX's behavior matches NumPy's for numpy version before 2.4.0.

Also note that the `lcm` bug is present in the most recent NumPy release:
```python
In [1]: import numpy as np

In [2]: np.__version__
Out[2]: '2.5.3'

In [3]: x_min = np.int32(np.iinfo(np.int32).min)

In [4]: np.lcm(x_min, 3)
Out[4]: np.int32(-2147483648)
```
